supplement.where: Online appendix at https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2023.18430 (Supplemental Material, PDF p. 2, journal p. 1589). The supplied PDF and markdown end with references and author biographies; the online appendix was not reviewed.
supplement.holds: Contents described in the main text: Appendix A, LLM inference (PDF p. 5, journal p. 1592), including A.2 on sampling (PDF p. 8, journal p. 1595); Appendix B, generation prompts, and Appendix C, evaluator survey instruments (PDF p. 9, journal p. 1596); Appendix D, regression results without controls (PDF p. 11, journal p. 1598); Appendix E, further text analysis of HC and HAI solutions (PDF p. 14, journal p. 1601). Tables 3-6 in the supplied PDF report coefficients and standard errors for the main controlled HC-versus-HAI models. The single-versus-multiple-instance post hoc comparisons are reported with p-values only; their contrast standard errors are not given in the main text. Additional appendix statistics cannot be confirmed without the supplement.

paper_design_summary: The authors ran a Freelancer.com challenge with Continuum Laboratory for circular-economy business ideas, retaining 125 eligible crowd solutions, and one author prompted GPT-4 in separate-instance and single-instance configurations to generate a reported 730 solutions (the source's generation counts are inconsistent; see notes). The analysis used 234 randomly selected solutions (54 crowd and 90 per GPT-4 configuration), arranged in 18 blocks of 13 and rated on five-point scales for novelty, strategic viability, environmental value, financial value, and overall quality by 300 analyzed US Prolific evaluators who passed screening and were randomly assigned one block each, blind to source (PDF pp. 8-10 and 12, journal pp. 1595-1597 and 1599). No person was randomly assigned to AI assistance; this is a comparison of researcher-prompted AI output with crowd output.

studies.label: Crowd solutions versus GPT-4 solutions from one author's prompts for a circular-economy business-idea challenge

assignment.what_was_assigned: No person was randomly assigned to work with or without AI or to an AI configuration. Solution source was determined by how it was produced: crowd submission or GPT-4 prompted by the same author in both configurations. Randomization concerned evaluation: 234 solutions were randomly selected from the 125 HC and reported 730 HAI solutions (54 HC and 90 per GPT-4 configuration), assigned to 18 blocks of 13 (3 HC, 5 multiple-instance, and 5 single-instance solutions from one prompting approach), and each of the 300 analyzed evaluators was randomly assigned one block. Every evaluator therefore rated solutions from all three sources; the between-source comparison is at the output level.
assignment.quote: comparing the novelty, value, and quality of solutions crowdsourced from humans to those generated by an individual strategically prompting a large language model (LLM)
assignment.locator: PDF p. 3 (journal p. 1590), Introduction; prompting by one author PDF p. 8 (journal p. 1595), Human-AI Collaboration and Prompt Engineering; random selection, blocks, and evaluator assignment PDF p. 9 (journal p. 1596), Evaluator Recruitment and Procedures, and PDF p. 10 (journal p. 1597), Figure 2

arms.name: Human crowd (HC)
arms.description: Solutions submitted to the crowdsourcing challenge run with Continuum Laboratory on Freelancer.com (January 30 to May 15, 2023); 125 deemed eligible after filtering, with 54 randomly selected and analyzed (Table 2: 54 ideas). The distinct solver count for those analyzed solutions and any solvers' use of AI tools are not stated. ai = none denotes no study-assigned AI assistance, not verified abstention (PDF pp. 8-9 and 12, journal pp. 1595-1596 and 1599).

arms.name: HAI multiple instance (independent search)
arms.description: GPT-4 solutions, each generated by a separate GPT-4 instance started from the default initialization; under the role-play prompts the solver profile or expert persona changed for each new instance. 90 solutions randomly selected and analyzed (Table 2: 90 ideas).

arms.name: HAI single instance (differentiated search)
arms.description: GPT-4 solutions generated one at a time in a single instance that kept all previous solutions in context, with a human-written differentiation instruction added after each output. 90 solutions randomly selected and analyzed (Table 2: 90 ideas).

participants.exclusions: Output producers: the contest received 310 submissions; 148 participants received $10 for nonblank entries; the research team deemed 125 of the 148 submissions eligible after filtering out off-topic or insufficiently detailed solutions. The abstract calls the challenge participants '125 global solvers', but the analysis used only 54 randomly selected HC solutions and does not explicitly state the number of distinct solvers represented in that subset. AI side: one author generated the GPT-4 solutions; the paper reports 730 in total and '315 each' per configuration, which are inconsistent, and 180 solutions were randomly selected and analyzed (90 per configuration). Raters, excluded from the output-producer count: 1,000 recruited on Prolific; 300 passed screening and were analyzed (145 from July 2023 and 155 from September 2023), yielding 3,900 evaluator-solution pairs. No count of people randomized to AI assistance is reported.
participants.who: Output producers: 'global solvers from various industries' who entered a Freelancer.com challenge (HC arm), and one study author prompting GPT-4 (HAI arms). Raters: US adults (18+) on Prolific screened for at least moderate interest plus either two or more years of work experience or at least 3 of 5 on a circular-economy skills test.
participants.country: Solvers: global (countries not listed); raters: United States
participants.quote: Of these, 180 were HAI prompt engineered (90 single instance and 90 multiple instance), and 54 were HC submitted.
participants.locator: PDF p. 9 (journal p. 1596), Evaluator Recruitment and Procedures; recruitment and filtering PDF p. 8 (journal p. 1595), Crowdsourcing Context; abstract PDF p. 2 (journal p. 1589); analyzed idea counts PDF p. 12 (journal p. 1599), Table 2

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI GPT-4 via the Python API, default temperature 1.0 (mid-2023)
ai_tool.how_used: One author wrote all prompts and GPT-4 generated complete solutions; no recruited solver was assigned AI assistance, and any independent AI use by crowd solvers is not reported. Two configurations: multiple instances (independent search) and a single instance that kept prior solutions in context with a differentiation instruction after each output (differentiated search). Three layered prompting approaches: a baseline (problem description, one-shot example, evaluation criteria, chain-of-thought-like wording), role-play with individual solver profiles, and role-play with famous expert personas from 23 industries. A reported 730 solutions (generation-count inconsistency noted below), 27.2 seconds and $0.037 each on average ($27.01 in total). Sources: PDF pp. 8-9 (journal pp. 1595-1596), Human-AI Collaboration and Prompt Engineering and API Costs and Time Spent.

task.description: Propose a sustainable, circular-economy business idea in a problem-solution format; solvers were told solutions would be judged on novelty, strategic viability, environmental value, financial value, and overall quality.
task.duration: Challenge ran January 30 to May 15, 2023. The paper states the HC solutions cost $2,555 and 2,520 hours and the final HAI solutions 5.5 hours and $27.01; GPT-4 took 27.2 seconds per solution on average. Sources: PDF p. 8 (journal p. 1595), Crowdsourcing Context; PDF p. 9 (journal p. 1596), API Costs and Time Spent; PDF p. 15 (journal p. 1602), Discussion.

outcomes.name: Novelty rating
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Five-point Likert rating by 300 analyzed Prolific evaluators who passed screening, blind to source: 'How different is it from existing solutions?' Each evaluator rated the 13 solutions of one randomly assigned block. Nested mixed-effects (hierarchical linear) models in lmerTest with random effects for evaluators and solution blocks, controlling for screening criteria, evaluator demographics, cohort, and solution word count. Results without controls are in online Appendix D (not in this PDF). The top-rating indicator is recorded separately as S1-O6. Rating items and scales: PDF p. 10 (journal p. 1597), Evaluator Recruitment and Procedures and Dependent Variables; model specification: PDF p. 11 (journal p. 1598), Estimation Approach.

company_involvement.description: The challenge was run in partnership with Continuum Laboratory, an AI company, and Freelancer.com, an online marketplace. Coauthor Vladimir Jacimovic lists Harvard Business School and ContinuumLab.AI as affiliations, and his bio calls him CEO and founder of ContinuumLab.ai. Coauthor Miaomiao Zhang is also listed with the ContinuumLab.AI affiliation on the title page, while her bio describes her as a PhD student at Harvard Business School. Funding came from Harvard Business School and the Laboratory for Innovation Science at Harvard.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 7 (journal p. 1594), Crowdsourcing Context; PDF p. 2 (journal p. 1589), author affiliations and Funding; PDF p. 20 (journal p. 1607), author bios

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is not met: one author prompted GPT-4 in both configurations, while crowd solutions came from a separate challenge (PDF p. 8, journal p. 1595, Human-AI Collaboration and Prompt Engineering). Randomization selected solutions and assigned evaluators to rating blocks; it did not assign people to AI assistance (PDF p. 9, journal p. 1596, Evaluator Recruitment and Procedures). Criterion 2 is unclear: the abstract reports 125 global solvers for the challenge, but only 54 HC solutions were analyzed and the distinct solver count for that subset is not explicitly stated; the 180 analyzed HAI solutions were generated by one author, and the 300 analyzed evaluators are raters, not output producers (PDF pp. 2, 8-9 and 12, journal pp. 1589, 1595-1596 and 1599; Table 2). The analyzed number of people therefore cannot be confirmed against the 50-person threshold. Criterion 3 is met: blinded evaluators rated the produced solutions on novelty and value/quality using a five-point scale (PDF p. 10, journal p. 1597, Evaluator Recruitment and Procedures and Dependent Variables). The missing solver count can change criterion 2 but cannot make this study core-eligible because criterion 1 is not met.

one_line_finding: Blind ratings from 300 analyzed Prolific evaluators (3,900 evaluator-solution pairs) scored GPT-4 solutions from one author's prompts lower than crowd solutions on novelty (-0.140, SE 0.035) and on the chance of a top novelty rating (-0.079, SE 0.012) but higher on strategic viability (0.088, SE 0.037), environmental value (0.160, SE 0.029), financial value (0.143, SE 0.033), and overall quality (0.101, SE 0.032), and the single-instance configuration showed no novelty difference from the crowd (-0.056, p = 0.156) (Tables 3-5, PDF pp. 12-13, journal pp. 1599-1600).
open_questions: Online Appendices D and E were not supplied: the main text says D contains results without controls and E contains further text analysis (PDF pp. 11 and 14, journal pp. 1598 and 1601). Reviewing the supplement would establish any additional outcome statistics or similarity/diversity measures. This cannot repair absent random assignment, and output scoring is already established.

Number of distinct crowd solvers represented in the 54 analyzed HC solutions, and thus the total analyzed output-producer count, is not explicitly reported (PDF p. 9, journal p. 1596; Table 2, PDF p. 12, journal p. 1599). Author confirmation of the distinct solver count or a solution-to-solver mapping would settle criterion 2. The 125-solvers abstract count refers to the challenge, and the 300 analyzed raters do not count; core remains no because criterion 1 fails.

Whether crowd solvers independently used AI tools is not reported in the challenge methods (PDF pp. 8-9, journal pp. 1595-1596). Authors could confirm the contest rules and any recorded use. This affects the interpretation of the HC comparator, but cannot change criterion 1 because AI assistance was not randomized, or the already met output criterion. ai = none means no study-assigned AI; mixed does not verify that HC outputs were AI-free.

Table 2 does not label its parenthesized values or specify the p-value test or how the top decile was formed (PDF p. 12, journal p. 1599; descriptive-statistics text PDF pp. 10-11). Authors could define these quantities. The printed means, parentheses and p-values are retained, but arm_means_sds_ns is removed because SDs are unconfirmed; eligibility does not depend on these details.

The source reports 730 generated AI solutions and 315 in each of two configurations (PDF p. 9, journal p. 1596), conflicting quality p-values in text and Table 2 (PDF pp. 10 and 12, journal pp. 1597 and 1599), and a top-strategic-viability coefficient/SE/p-value combination of -0.009, 0.031 and 0.469 (Table 6 and text, PDF p. 14, journal p. 1601). Author clarification would settle the intended values; the printed values are retained and none of these discrepancies affects eligibility.
notes: Pages are PDF pages; PDF p. 1 is the INFORMS cover page, so PDF p. N = journal p. N + 1587. The markdown conversion renders minus signs and equals signs as a replacement character; every sign and table value was checked against the PDF. Internal inconsistencies as printed: (1) PDF p. 10 (journal p. 1597) text gives 'single instance: p = 0.011' for quality vs. HC, while Table 2 prints 0.007 vs. HC and 0.011 vs. multiple instance; (2) Table 6 Model 2 prints SE (0.031) for HAI Multiple Instance (-0.009), out of line with the other HAI-coefficient SEs in Table 6 (0.011 to 0.015), and the text gives p = 0.469; recorded as printed; (3) PDF p. 9 (journal p. 1596) says '730 AI solutions, 315 each with multiple and single instances', and 315 + 315 = 630, while 730 agrees with the stated $0.037 average cost and $27.01 total; (4) the table notes print '****p < 0.1'. Table 2 parenthesized values are unlabeled, Table 2 p-values have no stated test, and Table 2 counts are ideas (54, 90, 90). The research team filtered out irrelevant and off-topic HC solutions before evaluation (PDF p. 15, journal p. 1602). The coauthor who prompted GPT-4 'possesses deep technical expertise in prompt engineering' (PDF p. 16, journal p. 1603). The paper calls its raters crowd rather than domain experts (PDF p. 16, journal p. 1603), so measure = human_raters. The acknowledgments state the authors used GPT-4 and Claude-3 for writing assistance. Primary status: both screeners coded not_stated; the final form uses paper_primary for the five ratings the paper calls its 'five main dependent variables' and secondary for the five top-rating indicators. Finalization: no c003 challenge files were present, so challenge_resolution is empty and all three challenge counts are zero. Counts after screening or output selection are described as analyzed, and unknown distinct-person counts remain null. Overall quality remains usefulness under the current codebook. The supplement description now distinguishes available HC-versus-HAI model SEs from unreported SEs for post hoc comparisons between AI configurations. All reconciliation differences are marked resolved; the reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as the prior review record, while final.open_items records current dispositions of its remaining factual uncertainties.

open_items.item: Resolved: overall quality remains usefulness under codebook section 6; the rating asks for overall quality based on novelty and three value criteria (PDF p. 10, journal p. 1597). Either construct label leaves criterion 3 met; no additional source is needed.

Online Appendices D and E were not supplied: the main text says D contains results without controls and E contains further text analysis (PDF pp. 11 and 14, journal pp. 1598 and 1601). Reviewing the supplement would establish any additional outcome statistics or similarity/diversity measures. This cannot repair absent random assignment, and output scoring is already established.

Resolved: single-versus-multiple-instance contrasts are coded other because codebook section 5 defines ai_design for randomized experiments; the same author prompted both GPT-4 configurations without random assignment of people (PDF p. 8, journal p. 1595). Their results remain recorded as context evidence. No additional source is needed.

Number of distinct crowd solvers represented in the 54 analyzed HC solutions, and thus the total analyzed output-producer count, is not explicitly reported (PDF p. 9, journal p. 1596; Table 2, PDF p. 12, journal p. 1599). Author confirmation of the distinct solver count or a solution-to-solver mapping would settle criterion 2. The 125-solvers abstract count refers to the challenge, and the 300 analyzed raters do not count; core remains no because criterion 1 fails.

Whether crowd solvers independently used AI tools is not reported in the challenge methods (PDF pp. 8-9, journal pp. 1595-1596). Authors could confirm the contest rules and any recorded use. This affects the interpretation of the HC comparator, but cannot change criterion 1 because AI assistance was not randomized, or the already met output criterion. ai = none means no study-assigned AI; mixed does not verify that HC outputs were AI-free.

Table 2 does not label its parenthesized values or specify the p-value test or how the top decile was formed (PDF p. 12, journal p. 1599; descriptive-statistics text PDF pp. 10-11). Authors could define these quantities. The printed means, parentheses and p-values are retained, but arm_means_sds_ns is removed because SDs are unconfirmed; eligibility does not depend on these details.

The source reports 730 generated AI solutions and 315 in each of two configurations (PDF p. 9, journal p. 1596), conflicting quality p-values in text and Table 2 (PDF pp. 10 and 12, journal pp. 1597 and 1599), and a top-strategic-viability coefficient/SE/p-value combination of -0.009, 0.031 and 0.469 (Table 6 and text, PDF p. 14, journal p. 1601). Author clarification would settle the intended values; the printed values are retained and none of these discrepancies affects eligibility.
